nameStory: This tiny sea slug earned its cheerful name from its bright yellow coloration that resembles a small drop of lemon juice against the rocky seafloor. The vibrant yellow color comes from specialized cells that concentrate yellow pigments, making these little creatures look like living citrus drops scattered across the ocean bottom.
description: The lemon drop is a small sea slug, technically called a nudibranch, that lives in New England's coastal waters. These soft-bodied marine animals are typically only about half an inch long and lack the protective shell that snails and other mollusks have. Instead, they rely on their bright yellow warning coloration and toxic compounds in their skin for protection. Their body is smooth and somewhat flattened, with a distinct head region and feathery gills arranged in a circle on their back.

idTips.label: Bright yellow coloration
idTips.description: The entire body is a vibrant lemon-yellow color, sometimes with subtle orange tinges, making it stand out dramatically against dark rocks and seaweed

idTips.label: Circular gill arrangement
idTips.description: Look for a crown of 6-9 feathery, branched gills arranged in a perfect circle on the back end of the animal - these retract quickly when disturbed

idTips.label: Smooth, soft texture
idTips.description: The body feels gelatinous and smooth to gentle touch, lacking any bumps, ridges, or hard shell - like touching firm jelly

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Typically measures only 10-15mm (about half an inch) long, roughly the size of a large pea when fully extended

idTips.label: Two horn-like tentacles
idTips.description: The head bears two club-shaped tentacles called rhinophores that can be withdrawn into sheaths - these help the animal smell and taste the water

habitat: Lemon drops are found in rocky intertidal zones and shallow subtidal areas along New England's coast, typically at depths of 3-30 feet. They prefer areas with good water circulation around rocky ledges, under overhangs, and among kelp forests where they can find their preferred food - sponges. Look for them attached to rocks, pilings, and jetties, especially in areas with encrusting sponges.

seasonality.spring: Adults become more active as water temperatures rise, and this is prime time for spotting them feeding on sponges in shallow tide pools during very low tides.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most likely to be seen, often in slightly deeper water as they follow their sponge prey. Mating and egg-laying occurs during warm months.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move to slightly deeper, more protected areas. Young animals from summer breeding may be visible as tiny yellow specks.
seasonality.winter: Much less active and typically found in deeper water or very sheltered locations. Rarely seen during this season without scuba diving.

funFact: Lemon drops are essentially living chemistry labs - they can steal toxic compounds from the sponges they eat and concentrate these poisons in their own skin, making their bright yellow color a warning sign that says 'I taste terrible and might make you sick!' to potential predators.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other yellow sea slugs, but the lemon drop's perfectly circular arrangement of gills on the back distinguishes it from other species. Remember: 'Lemon drops have gills arranged like flower petals in a perfect circle' - other yellow nudibranchs typically have different gill arrangements or body projections.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'sea slug,' nudibranchs like the lemon drop are actually highly specialized marine snails that have evolved to lose their shells. The term 'nudibranch' literally means 'naked gills,' referring to their exposed breathing structures, and these animals represent some of the most colorful and diverse groups in the ocean.
compareHints: Since this is the only Doriopsilla species in New England waters, compare it to other yellow dorid nudibranchs in the family. Unlike related species, the lemon drop maintains its bright, uniform yellow coloration throughout its life and has a distinctly circular gill crown rather than the more scattered or linear gill arrangements seen in similar species. The smooth texture and lack of any bumps or projections also helps distinguish it from other yellow sea slugs in the region.
